slides.title: Requirements
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Requirements

There are different classes of requirements:

e Data Independence

> application is shielded from physical storage

> physical storage can be reorganized

> hardware can be changed

e Scalability

> must scale to (nearly) arbitrary data sizes

P fast retrieval

P efficient access to individual data items

P updating arbitrary data

e Reliability

> data must never be lost

> must cope with hardware and software failures

slides.title: Layer Architecture
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Layer Architecture

e implementing all these requirements on the “bare metal” is hard

e and not desirable

e a DBMS must be maintainable and extensible

Instead: use a layer architecture

e the DBMS logic is split into levels of functionality

e each level is implemented by a specific layer

e each layer interacts only with the next lower layer

e simplifies and modularizes the code

The number of transistors on a chip doubles every 18 month.

Indirectly drove a number of other parameters:

e main memory size

e CPU speed

slides.slide_text_ocr:
Memory Hierarchy (2)

There are huge gaps between hierarchy levels

e traditionally, main memory vs. disk is most important

e but memory vs. cache etc. also relevant

The DBMS must aim to maximize locality.

slides.title: Hard Disk Access
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Hard Disk Access

Hard Disks are still the dominant external storage:

e

rotating platters, mechanical effects

e

transfer rate: ca. 150MB/s

e

seek time ca. 3ms

e

huge imbalance in random vs. sequential I/O!

The DBMS must take these effects into account

e sequential access is much more efficient

e gap is growing instead of shrinking

e even SSDs are slightly asymmetric (and have other problems)

slides.title: Hard Disk Access (2)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Hard Disk Access (2)

Techniques to speed up disk access:

e

do not move the head for every single tuple

e

instead, load larger chunks

e

typical granularity: one page

e

page size varies. traditionally 4KB, nowadays often 16K and more

e

page size is a trade-off

5

1

PE EI

slides.title: Hard Disk Access (3)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Hard Disk Access (3)

The page structure is very prominent within the DBMS

e granularity of I/O

e granularity of buffering/memory management

e granularity of recovery

Page is still too small to hide random I/O though

e sequential page access is important

e DBMSs use read-ahead techniques

e asynchronous write-back

slides.title: Buffer Management
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Management

Some pages are accessed very frequently

e reduce I/O by buffering/caching

e buffer manager keeps active pages in memory

e limited size, discards/write back when needed

e coupled with recovery, in particular logging

Basic interface:

1. FIX(pageNo,shared)

2. UNFIX(pageNo, dirty)

Pages can only be accessed (or modified) when they are fixed

slides.title: Buffer Replacement
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement

When memory is full, some buffer pages have to be replaced

e clean pages can be simply discarded

e dirty pages have to be written back first

e discarded pages are replaced with new pages

slides.title: Buffer Replacement - FIFO
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement - FIFO

First In - First Out

simple replacement strategy

buffer frames are kept in a linked list

inserted at the end, remove from the head

“old” pages are removed first

Does not take locality into account.

slides.title: Buffer Replacement - LRU
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement - LRU

Least Recently Used

e similar to FIFO, buffer frames are kept in a double-linked list

e remove from the head

e when a frame is unfixed, move it to the end of the list

e “hot” pages are kept in the buffer

A very popular strategy. Latching requires some care.

slides.title: Buffer Replacement - LFU
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement - LFU

Least Frequently Used

e remembers the number of access per page

e in-frequently used pages are remove first

e maintains a priority queue of pages

Sounds plausible, but too expensive in practice

slides.title: Buffer Replacement - Second Chance
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement - Second Chance

LRU is nice, but the LRU list is a hot spot.

Idea: use a simpler mechanism to simulate LRU

e

one bit per page

e

bit is set when page is unfixed

e

when replacing, replace pages with unset bit

set bits are cleared during the process

strategy is called “second chance” or “clock”

Easy to implement, but a bit crude.

slides.title: Buffer Replacement - 2Q
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement - 2Q

Maintain not one queue but two

e

many pages are referenced only once

e

some pages are hot and reference frequently

e

maintain a separate list for those

maintain all pages in FIFO queue

when a page is references again that is currently in FIFO, move it into an LRU queue

prefer evicting from FIFO

Hot pages are in LRU, read-once pages in FIFO. Good strategy for common DBMS operations.

slides.title: Buffer Replacement - Hints
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Buffer Replacement - Hints

Application knowledge can help buffer replacement

e 2Q tries to recognize read-once pages

e these occur when scanning over data

e but the DBMS knows this anyway!

e it could therefore give hints when unfixing

e e.g., will-need, or will-not-need (changes placement in queue)
